unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Good food is one of the best gifts a family shares each day. In this unit you learn to talk about food and health in English. You read about where food comes from, how to keep it clean and safe, and why fresh food helps your body and your brain. You give clear instructions, ask good questions, and compare healthy and unhealthy choices. Along the way you meet twenty new words, from sandwich and rice to pesticide and famine, and you use grammar that explains rules, reasons and comparisons. By the end you are ready for this unit's story, The Bitter Lunch, about a girl named Amal who learns to check her food with care.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary groups. Learn a few words each day and tick your Word Wall.
Work through the six short grammar lessons, one at a time.
Read the four texts and the story The Bitter Lunch, then answer the comprehension questions.
Work through the four skills in order: Reading and listening, then Speaking, then Writing, then Activities.
Finish with the checkpoint quiz and the Self-Assessment to see what you have learned.

readings.title: From Farm to Plate
readings.setting: A river-valley farming village and familiar learner settings
readings.passageScript:
Every meal begins far away from your plate. In Amal's village beside the river, farmers rise before dawn to begin the day's labour. Some farmers grow rice in wet, flooded fields, while others keep cattle in the dry, grassy fields on higher ground. Growing food takes patience: farmers plant seeds, wait for rain, and pull weeds for many weeks before harvest. Their labour starts early in the morning and ends when the sun goes down.
When the rice is ripe and the animals are ready, the food begins a long journey. First it travels to the market, where food is bought and sold. From the market, some food goes on to the bakery, where bread is made fresh each day. Only after this journey does the food finally reach your home.
Fresh food is full of goodness. It helps your body grow strong and helps your brain think clearly. But food must be kept clean and safe the whole way from farm to plate. Sometimes farmers use pesticide to stop insects from eating the crops before they can be picked. A little pesticide can protect the plants, but too many chemicals sprayed on food can be harmful to people, animals and the land.
That is why we must always wash fruit and vegetables before we eat them, and why farmers work so hard, even during a famine, to make sure no family goes hungry.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: A Poster on the Wall
readings.setting: A river-valley farming village and familiar learner settings
readings.passageScript:
Teacher Yasmin put a new health poster on the classroom wall this week, and she asked every child to read it carefully before break time. In neat, bold letters, the poster said:
Eat fresh food to stay strong. Choose rice, lamb, fruit and vegetables instead of sweets from the shop.
Wash your hands before you eat, and wash every piece of fruit as well, because dust and pesticide can hide on the skin.
Drink clean water every day to help your brain and your stomach work well.
Gather your family at the table and share a meal together whenever you can.
Fresh fruit is better than sweets, so keep sweets for special days only.
Never eat food that smells strange, or comes from a bakery shelf that has sat out for too long.
At the bottom, Teacher Yasmin had written one more line in red pen: “A healthy body starts with a healthy plate. Ask an adult if you are ever unsure about a food.” Amal read the poster twice and copied her favourite line into her notebook, remembering to add a comma after every item in her list.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: At the Clinic
readings.setting: A river-valley farming village and familiar learner settings
readings.passageScript:
Doctor Sarah: “Good morning, Amal. How do you feel today?”
Amal: “Not very well, Doctor Sarah. My stomach hurts, and I feel a little dizzy.”
Doctor Sarah: “I am sorry to hear that. Can you tell me what you ate?”
Amal: “I ate an old sandwich last night. It had meat, chewy cheese and spice inside.”
Doctor Sarah: “Was the meat fresh?”
Amal: “No. It was not fresh, and it smelled strange, but I was very hungry, so I ate it anyway.”
Doctor Sarah: “That was not a wise choice. When meat is not fresh, chemicals can build up inside it, and that can make your stomach very unhappy.”
Amal: “I did not know that. What should I do now?”
Doctor Sarah: “Drink plenty of clean water, and rest at home today instead of going to school. You must be more careful. Old food might make you very sick. Always check your food first.”
Amal: “I will remember that, Doctor Sarah. Thank you for helping me.”
Doctor Sarah: “You are welcome, Amal. Tell your grandmother to gather only fresh food from the market from now on, and you will feel strong again soon.”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: The Bitter Lunch
readings.setting: A river-valley farming village and familiar learner settings
readings.passageScript:
Amal lived beside the river, where the fields were hot and green. She helped Grandma Hana grow rice and care for the cattle. Every morning before school, she fed the cows and carried water from the well. It was hard labour. Grandma Hana always smiled and said, “We work hard now to eat well later.”
One day at school, Teacher Yasmin stood at the front of the class. “I have a project for you,” she said. “Each of you will write a story about food, and it must carry a health message. You must use our new words and write with care. You might even share your story at the community lunch.”
Amal raised her hand. “Can it be a true story?” she asked.
“Yes,” Teacher Yasmin said, “as long as it teaches something helpful.”
That evening, Amal walked to the village bakery. It smelled of warm bread. She was hungry, so she bought a sandwich of salty meat, chewy cheese and spice.
“I should tell you,” said Omar the baker, “this meat is not fresh. It still tastes good, though.” Amal was too hungry to care.
At home, she shared part of the sandwich with her cousin Noah. He frowned. “I think this meat is from sick cattle,” he said. “There is a strange smell.”
“You worry too much,” said Amal, and she ate the rest.
Late that night, Amal's stomach hurt badly. She felt heat in her belly and cold in her hands, and she could not sleep. Noah heard her groaning and woke the family.
At the clinic, Doctor Sarah checked her carefully. “This may be food poisoning,” she said. “Some chemicals are used to clean old meat. They are dangerous if nobody washes them off.”
Amal groaned. “I only ate a sandwich. It had a lot of spice, but the meat may have been old.”
“You must be more careful,” said Doctor Sarah gently. “Old meat and dirty tools can lead to disease. Eaten too often, bad food can even lead to a serious sickness like cancer. Always check your food first.”
The next day, Amal stayed home from school. Grandma Hana brought her warm soup and said, “You are lucky this was not deadly. Always check what you eat.”
By the afternoon, Amal felt better. Then she remembered her story. She sat outside with her notebook and wrote:
“I once ate a bad sandwich. It looked fine, but it was not fresh. It gave me a sore stomach, and I learned to check what I eat.”
She thought for a while, then wrote more: “Some chemicals help to clean food, but too much is harmful. Farmers must use less pesticide, and people must wash their food with care.”
“What else should I write?” she asked Noah.
“Gather some facts about food and health,” he said. “Then give good advice.”
Amal smiled. “That helps.” She added one last part: “We eat to feed our brain and our body, and good food helps us grow. Too much alcohol or dirty food can make us sick. A famine shows us how precious food really is, and how we must protect it.”
On the day of the community lunch, Amal read her story aloud. A few children laughed at first, until she reached the part about her illness. Then the room grew quiet, and everyone listened.
“Thank you for that, Amal,” said Teacher Yasmin. “Now, who else would like to share?”
Noah raised his hand. “Amal also learned where to put a comma in a list of food!” The whole room giggled.
Then Grandma Hana stood up. “Food costs months of labour, so let us never waste it,” she said. “Let us never eat without checking it first, either.”
The lunch was lamb, rice and sweet dates. Amal chose only what looked clean and safe. The meal was simple, but everything was warm and fresh.
Amal leaned over to Noah. “This is the freshest lamb I have had in weeks,” she whispered.
He grinned. “That is because I helped to cook it.”
Amal took a bite and smiled. This time, her stomach did not hurt at all.

comprehension.question: In From Farm to Plate, name the two jobs the farmers do in the wet fields and the dry ones.
comprehension.correctAnswer: They grow rice in the wet fields and keep cattle in the dry ones.
comprehension.explanation: The second sentence pairs the two jobs, giving rice to the wet fields and cattle to the dry ones.

comprehension.question: Which two places does the food pass through before it finally reaches your home?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It travels to the market and then the bakery before it reaches your home.
comprehension.explanation: The text lists the journey in order: the market first, the bakery next, and home last.

comprehension.question: Write down two command verbs that begin the advice on the classroom poster.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Any two of these command verbs: Eat, Wash, Drink.
comprehension.explanation: Each line of the poster opens with the base verb, which is what makes it an imperative.

comprehension.question: Copy the one comparison the poster makes, and say which food it prefers.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Fresh fruit is better than sweets, so the poster prefers fresh fruit.
comprehension.explanation: Only one line uses better than, and the food named before better than is the one preferred.

comprehension.question: At the clinic, what does Amal say she ate the night before?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says she ate an old sandwich the night before.
comprehension.explanation: Amal answers the first question by naming the old sandwich as the cause of her sore stomach.

comprehension.question: Which sentence in the clinic talk gives a rule, and which one gives a possibility?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The rule is “You must be more careful” and the possibility is “Old food might make you very sick”.
comprehension.explanation: Must marks the rule the doctor sets, while might marks something that may or may not happen.

comprehension.question: Which three foods does The Market Song ask you to gather with care?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The song names rice, lamb and fresh green peas.
comprehension.explanation: The three foods appear in the opening line, joined by and before the word gather.

comprehension.question: According to the last line of the song, what does healthy food help children do?
comprehension.explanation: The closing line gives the reason for washing and cooking the food carefully.

comprehension.question: What two jobs does Amal do each morning before school in The Bitter Lunch?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She feeds the cows and carries water from the well.
comprehension.explanation: Both jobs appear in the opening paragraph, before Grandma Hana speaks about working hard.

comprehension.question: Why did the sandwich make Amal ill, and what did Doctor Sarah say caused it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The meat was not fresh, and Doctor Sarah blamed chemicals used to clean old meat that were not washed off.
comprehension.explanation: Omar warns about the meat early on, and the doctor names the unwashed cleaning chemicals later.

comprehension.question: What health message does Amal finally write into her own story?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She writes that farmers must use less pesticide and that people must wash their food with care.
comprehension.explanation: Amal adds this advice after Noah tells her to gather facts and then give good advice.

comprehension.question: At the community lunch, how does Amal choose her food, and what has changed her?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She chooses only what looks clean and safe, because her illness taught her to check food first.
comprehension.explanation: The ending mirrors the beginning: the same girl who ignored a warning now checks before she eats.

grammar.title: Modal Verbs — must and might
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs are special helping verbs, and this unit uses two of them. Must shows that something is necessary or very important, like a rule. Might shows that something is possible, but not certain.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
must → subject + must + base verb: “You must wash fresh fruit.”
might → subject + might + base verb: “Pesticides might harm plants.”
Negatives: mustn't means not allowed, as in “You mustn't eat old meat.”
might not means probably will not, as in “Nora might not come today.”
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write “You must to wash your hands.” After must or might, use the base verb with no to: “You must wash your hands.”
grammar.memoryTip: Must is a strong rule from a teacher, and might is a gentle maybe from a friend.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with must or might: | You ______ finish your lunch before going outside. (a rule) | It ______ rain tomorrow, so take a jacket! (a possibility) | We ______ wash the vegetables before we cook them. (a rule) | Noah ______ go to the market later if he has time. (a possibility) Self-check: 1. must, 2. might, 3. must, 4. might.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Yes/No Questions
grammar.explanation: A Yes/No question can be answered with yes or no, so it gets you clear, direct information about food and health.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Start with a helping verb (is, are, do, does, can), then the subject, then the rest.
Is alcohol bad for health?
Does rice grow in water?
Are you hungry?
Can we buy bread at the bakery?
Use do with I, you, we and they. Use does with he, she and it.
grammar.commonMistake: “Does he eats breakfast?” keeps an extra s on the verb. After does, use the base verb: “Does he eat breakfast?”
grammar.memoryTip: Say the word order like a little rhyme: helping verb, subject, then the rest.
grammar.practice: Choose the correct helping verb (Do, Does, Are, Is) to start each question: | ______ cats eat fish? | ______ your brother like rice? | ______ they hungry now? | ______ it raining outside? | ______ you want more soup? Self-check: 1. Do, 2. Does, 3. Are, 4. Is, 5. Do.

grammar.title: The Infinitive of Purpose
grammar.explanation: The infinitive of purpose explains why we do something. In “We eat vitamins to stay healthy”, the words to stay healthy give the reason.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use to plus the base verb to give the reason.
Farmers work to grow crops.
We eat good food to help our brain and body.
Amal saves money to buy fresh fruit.
You can also use so that with a subject: “We wash food so that we do not get sick.”
grammar.commonMistake: “We eat vitamins staying healthy” drops the word to and uses the wrong verb form. Write “We eat vitamins to stay healthy.”
grammar.memoryTip: Picture to as a little bridge that joins the action to its reason, then cross it with a verb.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with to and the verb in brackets: | He exercises every day ______ (keep) fit. | Nora saves her money ______ (buy) fresh fruit. | We wash our hands ______ (stay) clean. | They study hard ______ (improve) their English. Self-check: 1. to keep, 2. to buy, 3. to stay, 4. to improve.

grammar.title: Imperatives (Giving Commands)
grammar.explanation: Imperatives are verbs that give a command, an instruction or advice, which is why recipes, posters and safety rules are full of them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use the base verb and leave out the subject you: Gather the cattle!
Add details to be clear: Avoid deadly plants. Carefully wash the meat.
To tell someone not to do something, use Don't: Don't eat old food.
Add please to sound polite: Please close the door.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing “You gather the cattle!” adds a subject the command does not need. Start with the verb: “Gather the cattle!”
grammar.memoryTip: An imperative is one clear order, like a coach shouting “Run!” or “Stop!”

grammar.title: Comparisons
grammar.explanation: Comparisons show how two things are the same or different, so they help you share an opinion and choose between two foods.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Short adjective with one syllable: add -er, so tall becomes taller and fresh becomes fresher.
Adjective ending in -y: change y to -ier, so happy becomes happier and healthy becomes healthier.
Long adjective with three or more syllables: use more, so delicious becomes more delicious.
Then add than: “Rice is cheaper than meat.”
Two special ones: good becomes better, and bad becomes worse. Fun is special too: we say more fun, not funner.
grammar.commonMistake: “She is more tall than her brother” uses more with a short adjective. Write “She is taller than her brother.” Remember than as well: not “This bus is faster”, but “This bus is faster than that one.”
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the rhyme: for one small word just add an -er, and for a long one use more, for sure.
grammar.practice: Write the correct comparison word: | This mango is ______ (sweet) than that one. | Fresh bread is ______ (good) than old bread. | Running is ______ (fun) than walking. | Summer is ______ (hot) than spring. Self-check: 1. sweeter, 2. better, 3. more fun, 4. hotter.

grammar.title: Wh- Questions
grammar.explanation: Wh- questions begin with what, who, where, when, why or how, and each one asks for a different kind of detail.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
What asks about things: “What do you like to eat?”
Who asks about people: “Who cooked the lamb?”
Where asks about places: “Where does rice grow?”
When asks about time: “When is dinner?”
Why asks for reasons: “Why is famine dangerous?”
How asks about the way something happens: “How do chemicals affect food?”
With the verb to be, the verb comes straight after the Wh- word: “Where is the bakery?”
grammar.commonMistake: “Why he is running?” leaves the subject in front of the verb. Swap them over: “Why is he running?”
grammar.memoryTip: Treat every Wh- word as a fishing rod that catches its own kind of answer.
grammar.practice: Complete each question with the correct Wh- word: | ______ do you want for lunch? | ______ is your favourite fruit? | ______ does rice grow? | ______ do we wash our food? (Ask for the reason.) | ______ do you feel today? Self-check: 1. What, 2. What, 3. Where, 4. Why, 5. How.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Food and Health Interview
speaking.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work with a partner and interview each other about food and health.
Ask three Yes/No questions, such as “Do you wash fruit before you eat it?”, and three Wh- questions, such as “Why is fresh food better?”
Answer in full sentences and use at least six unit words: bakery, cattle, pesticide, famine, stomach and brain.
Swap roles, then tell your partner which of their answers was the clearest.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult present, ask the tutor to be the person I interview and to correct my question word order.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Explain the Journey to Your Plate
speaking.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Retell the journey food takes from the farm to your plate, using From Farm to Plate to help you.
Sequence your talk with first, next, then and finally, and name the field, the market, the bakery and your home.
Give one reason with to plus a verb, such as “Farmers spray pesticide to protect the crops.”
Finish with one sentence about what people must do before they eat.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult nearby, ask the tutor to listen to my farm-to-plate talk and to check my order words.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: My Two-Minute Food Safety Talk
speaking.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Plan and record a two-minute talk called Checking My Food.
Open by saying why food safety matters, then give three checks a family can make before cooking.
Use one must sentence, one might sentence and one comparison, and end with the advice you would give Amal.
Listen to your recording once, then record it again and keep the better version.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult supervising, ask the tutor to score my two-minute food safety talk against clarity, vocabulary and a clear ending.

writing.title: Writing 1: How to Make a Sandwich (Instructions)
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write four to six steps that explain how to make a healthy sandwich.
Use command verbs and the order words first, next, then and finally.
Begin like this: First, wash your hands. Next, take two slices of fresh bread. Then, ______. Finally, ______.
Check that every step could be followed by someone who has never made a sandwich.
writing.modelText: Strong steps begin with a command verb, run in a sensible order, and name real ingredients such as fresh bread, cheese and washed salad.
writing.successCriteria: I used a command verb to start each step; I put the steps in order; I used first, next, then and finally; I named fresh ingredients; I checked my full stops
writing.support: Say the steps aloud while miming them, then write down the words you said.
writing.extension: Add one safety warning with must, such as “You must wash the salad first.”

writing.title: Writing 2: A Health Poster
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Design a poster titled Why Fresh Food is Important, with four short pieces of advice.
Three of them must be imperatives that would fit on a poster about safe, healthy food.
Include at least one comparison, such as “Fresh food is better than old food”, and one sentence that uses must.
Lay the poster out clearly, with the biggest words at the top.
writing.modelText: A strong poster mixes three short commands with one comparison, keeps each line under eight words, and puts the title in the largest letters.
writing.expectedLength: A title and four short lines
writing.successCriteria: I wrote three imperative lines; I used one comparison with than; I used must once; I kept each line short; I laid out the title clearly
writing.support: Copy two lines from the classroom poster first, then change the food words to your own.
writing.extension: Add a picture caption that explains your best piece of advice in one sentence.

writing.title: Writing 3: A Short Report
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write five to six sentences for a mini-report called How Pesticides Help and Harm.
Explain one way pesticide helps farmers and one way too many chemicals can harm people.
Use the words pesticide, chemicals and crops at least once each.
End the report with your own advice in a sentence that uses must.
writing.modelText: A strong report opens with a topic sentence, gives one benefit and one danger with a real example, and closes with clear advice using must.
writing.expectedLength: Five to six sentences in one paragraph
writing.successCriteria: I opened with a topic sentence; I gave one benefit; I gave one danger; I used the three key words; I ended with advice using must
writing.support: Reread From Farm to Plate and underline the two sentences about pesticide before you start.
writing.extension: Add a second paragraph about what farmers could use instead of pesticide.

writing.title: Writing 4: My Own Health Message
writing.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write your own short health message of three or four sentences, like the one Amal wrote.
Begin with the words “I learned to ______.”
Say what happened, what you learned, and what you do differently now.
Keep it true, and keep every sentence under sixteen words.
writing.modelText: A strong health message tells one small true event, names the lesson learned, and finishes with the habit the writer keeps today.
writing.successCriteria: I began with I learned to; I told one true event; I named what I learned; I said what I do now; I checked my capital letters
writing.support: Talk through your true event with an adult before you write the first sentence.
writing.extension: Rewrite your message as advice for a younger child, using two imperatives.

writing.title: Writing 5: From Farm to Plate Information Text
writing.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a heading and five accurate facts about where our food comes from.
Use the unit words cattle, labour, bakery, rice and famine, one in each fact.
Number the facts, and make each one a complete sentence that a reader could check.
Keep opinions out of this piece, because information texts report facts.
writing.modelText: A strong information text uses a clear heading, numbers each fact, keeps to one idea per fact, and uses precise words instead of vague ones.
writing.expectedLength: A heading and five numbered facts
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a clear heading; I numbered five facts; I used all five unit words; I kept each fact to one idea; I checked that every fact is true
writing.support: Find each unit word in From Farm to Plate and copy the sentence around it as a model.
writing.extension: Add a sixth fact that compares two of the places food travels through.

writing.title: Writing 6: Check, Correct and Improve
writing.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose one earlier piece of writing from this unit and improve it.
Revise three sentences so they are clearer, and add two useful unit words.
Check every list of three or more foods for commas, and check every sentence for a capital letter and a full stop.
Finish by drawing Amal at the community lunch and writing one caption sentence about the wise choice she made.
writing.modelText: A strong revision shows the old sentence and the better one side by side, and the caption names both the choice and the reason behind it.
writing.expectedLength: Three revised sentences and one caption
writing.successCriteria: I revised three sentences; I added two unit words; I checked my commas in lists; I checked capital letters and full stops; I wrote one caption sentence
writing.support: Read your old work aloud, and mark every place where you run out of breath.
writing.extension: Explain to a partner why each revision makes the sentence easier to read.

activities.title: Activities 1: True or False (Food and Health Facts)
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write True or False for each statement, and correct the false ones.
Fresh food is better for your body than old food.
You should never wash fruit before eating it.
A pesticide is a chemical that kills insects on plants.
Alcohol is a safe drink for children.
activities.answerSummary: Two statements are true and two are false; each false one must be rewritten as a correct sentence.

activities.title: Activities 2: Sort the Words
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Make two lists from these words: fresh, deadly, chewy, sandwich, rice, stomach.
Put the naming words (nouns) in one list and the describing words (adjectives) in the other.
Then write one sentence that uses a noun and an adjective from your lists together.
activities.answerSummary: Three words belong in each list, and the extra sentence must pair one word from each column.

activities.title: Activities 3: Fill in the Blanks (must / might)
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose must or might for each sentence, then say why you chose it.
You ______ wash your hands before you eat. (a rule)
It ______ rain later, so the farmers are working fast. (a possibility)
We ______ check that meat is fresh before we cook it. (a rule)
Nora ______ buy bread from the bakery if it is open. (a possibility)
activities.answerSummary: Rules take must and possibilities take might; the base verb follows with no to.

activities.title: Activities 4: Ask the Question
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write a Wh- question that each answer below would fit.
Answer: “Rice grows in wet fields.” (Begin with Where.)
Answer: “Farmers use pesticide to protect the crops.” (Begin with Why.)
Answer: “A famine happens when there is not enough food.” (Begin with What.)
activities.answerSummary: Each question must use the named Wh- word and put the helping verb before the subject.

activities.title: Activities 5: Commas in Food Lists
activities.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Copy each list and put the commas in the right places.
I like apples bananas and oranges.
We bought rice lamb and sweet dates at the market.
The bakery sells bread cakes and biscuits.
Then write your own list of four foods you would take on a picnic, using commas correctly.
activities.answerSummary: A comma separates each item in a list of three or more, and the last item follows and.

activities.title: Activities 6: Story Evidence Hunt
activities.origin: Curriculum-reviewed extension of the Grade 4 source
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Hunt for the evidence in The Bitter Lunch and write your answers in full sentences.
What project does Teacher Yasmin give the class?
What advice does Doctor Sarah give Amal about her food?
Find the sentence in the story that contains each of these words: cattle, bakery, chemicals, famine.
Copy one sentence you found and read it aloud with expression.
activities.answerSummary: Each answer must quote or closely follow the words of the story rather than a guess.

assignments.title: Food and Health learning portfolio
assignments.instructions:
Submit two pieces for your Food and Health portfolio: Writing 3, the short report on how pesticides help and harm, and a recording of Speaking 6, your two-minute food safety talk.
Improve both pieces first, using the Grade 4 writing and speaking rubrics.
Marking guidance for the teacher: award the sixteen writing marks for a clear topic sentence, one accurate benefit, one accurate danger, correct use of pesticide, chemicals and crops, and a closing sentence that uses must. Award the sixteen speaking marks for an audible opening, three family food checks in a sensible order, one must sentence, one might sentence, one comparison, and a closing piece of advice. Where a criterion is only partly met, award the level that matches the strongest evidence across the whole piece.

quizzes.question: Which word means a time when many people do not have enough food?
quizzes.explanation: A famine is a shortage of food, while a bakery is a shop, a spice is a flavouring and a comma is a punctuation mark.

quizzes.question: Which word names the chemical a farmer sprays to kill insects on crops?
quizzes.explanation: Pesticide is sprayed on plants; a stomach is a body part, a comma is a punctuation mark and labour is hard work.

quizzes.question: Amal had to chew the dried meat for a long time. Which unit word describes it?
quizzes.explanation: Chewy means hard to bite, so it fits meat that needs long chewing; fresh, deadly and famine describe other things.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from The Market Song: “Rice and ______ and fresh green peas, gather them with care, if you please!”
quizzes.explanation: The song lists three foods, and only lamb is a food that fits between rice and green peas.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses must correctly to give a rule?
quizzes.options: You must to wash the fruit. | You must wash the fruit. | You must washing the fruit. | You must washes the fruit.
quizzes.explanation: After must we use the base verb on its own, with no to, no -ing and no -s.

quizzes.question: Which helping verb correctly begins this question: ______ your brother like rice?
quizzes.explanation: Your brother is one person, so the question needs does with the base verb like.

quizzes.question: Which sentence gives the reason using to and a base verb?
quizzes.options: We wash the fruit for clean. | We wash the fruit before removing pesticide. | We wash the fruit to remove pesticide. | We wash the fruit so clean it.
quizzes.correctAnswer: We wash the fruit to remove pesticide.
quizzes.explanation: Only this sentence uses to plus the base verb remove, which is how the infinitive of purpose gives a reason.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is a correct imperative for a food-safety poster?
quizzes.options: You wash the fruit before eating. | The fruit is washed by you. | Washing the fruit is important for everyone. | Wash the fruit before you eat it.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Wash the fruit before you eat it.
quizzes.explanation: An imperative starts with the base verb and leaves out the subject you.

quizzes.question: Which sentence compares two kinds of bread correctly?
quizzes.options: Fresh bread is better than old bread. | Fresh bread is more good than old bread. | Fresh bread is gooder than old bread. | Fresh bread is the most good bread.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Fresh bread is better than old bread.
quizzes.explanation: Good has the special comparison form better, and a comparison needs than to join the two things.

quizzes.question: Which food list uses commas correctly?
quizzes.options: We bought rice lamb and dates. | We bought, rice lamb and dates. | We bought rice, lamb, and dates. | We, bought rice, lamb and dates.
quizzes.correctAnswer: We bought rice, lamb, and dates.
quizzes.explanation: A comma separates each item in a list of three or more, and no comma belongs after the verb bought.

teacherNotes.note: Model every new food word aloud and check meaning before independent work. Mix spoken, written and drawn responses so each learner can show what they know. Whenever the AI tutor is used, an adult stays in the room and closes the session at the end; no child works alone with the device. Handle the cancer and alcohol words factually and briefly, and let any learner step back from the topic. Give feedback on complete sentences, text evidence and precise vocabulary.

teacherNotes.noteType: Source-linked answer keys and AI tutor support
teacherNotes.note:
Grammar practice answers, taken from the source answer key.
Grammar 1 (must / might): 1. must 2. might 3. must 4. might.
Grammar 2 (Yes/No questions): 1. Do 2. Does 3. Are 4. Is 5. Do.
Grammar 3 (infinitive of purpose): 1. to keep 2. to buy 3. to stay 4. to improve.
Grammar 4 (imperatives): 1. Eat your vegetables! 2. Wash the fruit before you eat it. 3. Don't touch that hot pot! 4. Help your brother carry the rice.
Grammar 5 (comparisons): 1. sweeter 2. better 3. more fun 4. hotter.
Grammar 6 (Wh- questions): 1. What 2. What 3. Where 4. Why 5. How.
Reading answers: farmers grow rice in wet fields and keep cattle in dry ones; food travels to the market, the bakery and then home; pesticide stops insects eating the crops, but too many chemicals harm people; always wash fruit and vegetables first.
Poster answers: any two of Eat, Wash, Drink; the comparison is “Fresh fruit is better than sweets”; the favourite piece of advice is the learner's own, with a reason.
Suggested tutor prompts, with an adult present for every session.
Vocabulary: “Can you quiz me on the five food words?” · “Why is fresh food better for me than old food?”
Grammar: “Can you check my grammar answers?” · “Why do we say You must wash and not You must to wash?”
Reading: “Can you read From Farm to Plate with me and explain any hard words?” · “Can you ask me questions about The Bitter Lunch?”
Speaking and writing: “Can you play the Healthy or Not game with me?” · “Can you check that I used commas correctly in my food list?”

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: 1. True. 2. False, you should always wash fruit before eating it. 3. True. 4. False, alcohol is not safe for children. Award the mark only when the false items are rewritten correctly.
Nouns: sandwich, rice, stomach. Adjectives: fresh, deadly, chewy. A model pairing sentence is “The chewy sandwich filled my stomach.”
1. must 2. might 3. must 4. might. Rules take must and possibilities take might, and the verb after each stays in its base form.
1. Where does rice grow? 2. Why do farmers use pesticide? 3. What is a famine? Accept any wording that keeps the named Wh- word and puts the helping verb before the subject.

1. I like apples, bananas, and oranges. 2. We bought rice, lamb, and sweet dates at the market. 3. The bakery sells bread, cakes, and biscuits. The learner's own picnic list needs a comma after each of the first three foods.

The project is to write a story about food that carries a health message. Doctor Sarah's advice is to be more careful and to always check food first. The sentences to find contain cattle in the opening paragraph, bakery in the evening walk, chemicals in the clinic, and famine in Amal's final paragraph.
famine. A famine is a long shortage of food; check that the learner did not choose bakery, which is a place rather than a period of time.
pesticide. Ask the learner to name the insects it targets, then to say why washing the fruit still matters afterwards.
chewy. Point back to the sandwich in The Bitter Lunch, where the cheese needed a lot of chewing.
lamb. Say the whole line aloud so the learner hears that only a food fits between rice and green peas.
You must wash the fruit. Remind the learner that must is followed by the base verb, with no to, no -ing and no -s.
Does. Your brother is one person, so does is needed and the verb like stays in its base form.
We wash the fruit to remove pesticide. Underline to remove and ask which question it answers, which is why.
Wash the fruit before you eat it. An imperative drops the subject you and opens with the base verb.
Fresh bread is better than old bread. Good becomes better, never gooder or more good, and than joins the two breads.
We bought rice, lamb, and dates. Commas separate the three foods; there is never a comma straight after the verb bought.
